title: In No Respect Is the Father Greater than the Son
english: … intelligible realities, supposing that they are made like the flux of matter. For the things above the heavens all surpass every mind and every thought, while earthly things are lowly, and come to be and pass away in time.

But above all, he was born without beginning, co-existing and co-working with his own true Father, as light with the disc of the sun. And he has the witness of the Scriptures that he is God, Lord, holy, Creator, incorruptible, life, light, and everything that the Father is. And he ought rather to be granted likeness and equality from the many than unlikeness from the one.

And how did Adam and Eve, who were not begotten and had no father, come to be equal in nature to us who are descended from them? Or what comparison at all did they make of what they call ‘unlike’? Or by what measuring did they settle on ‘better and greater’, when Scripture neither divides by nature the holy, beginningless, one and undivided Trinity, nor marks off within it a first and a later? Two things are plain: that what is greater is not necessarily of another substance, and that comparatives, as a rule, are used of things of the same substance, not of things of different substance. Nor could they say anything to the point even by guesswork, since they cannot do so even about ‘incomparable and greater’.

It is not by size or any bulk. For God the Word is without size or breadth, and stands apart from all magnitude, composition and shape, as do the Father and his Holy Spirit; he himself is contained by nothing, but contains all things. For he is also the beginning of all magnitudes, as their maker. Where indeed is there size in the highest and superior hypostases, which are beyond even the incorporeal?

Nor is it in respect of being without beginning. For he co-exists with the Father as “the radiance of his glory” (Hebrews 1:3), and has no God before him. For indeed it says: “In the beginning was the Word” (John 1:1). And God, the Maker, is not measured by time alongside a thing made. For necessity demands of them, a thing perilous even to think, that they posit a time before the God and Father who is without beginning and beyond comprehension, and so make the comparison. People are accustomed to call ‘greater’ those who were born earlier in time, as when Isaac ordains: “The greater shall serve the lesser” (Genesis 25:23).

Nor is it as cause: for he is not his cause. For the only-begotten Son too has been shown to be without beginning; otherwise the Father would be greater than him in the same way as he is greater than us, which be it far from us to say or to hear.

Nor is it in substance and likeness. For he is from him “as the Only-begotten from the Father, full of grace and truth” (John 1:14), and as “the stamp of his hypostasis” (Hebrews 1:3), a stamp in every respect, and as “the image of God” (2 Corinthians 4:4; Colossians 1:15), of which it is said that “he who has seen it has seen the Father” (John 14:9). “For in him dwells all the fullness of the Godhead” (Colossians 2:9). And the words “Let us make man after our image and likeness” (Genesis 1:26) are also drawn in as witness to this.

Nor is it by a heightening of quality, since the divine and ineffable hypostases are not qualities. Quality is found in bodies, but they are incorporeal and intelligible. Indeed, it cannot even be thought of them that there is something more beautiful than the beautiful and better than the more beautiful, in the manner of Paul’s saying on another matter: “And now these three remain: faith, hope, love; but the greater of these is love” (1 Corinthians 13:13). For he assigned ‘greater’ to love because of its intensity toward virtue: having loved, he says, we believe, and having believed we hope to reign with Christ.

For if “one God” (1 Corinthians 8:6) is true, and “that you may become partakers of the divine nature” (2 Peter 1:4), not ‘of natures’, then it has been shown that the good, taken absolutely, is also one: I mean the Godhead.

Nor is it in respect of equality, because it is written that the Son is great and “God over all” (Romans 9:5), “making himself equal to the Father” (John 5:18), and “swearing by himself, since he has no one greater” (Hebrews 6:13).

Nor is it in power. For it is written: “Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God” (1 Corinthians 1:24), and “Whatever the Father does, the Son also does likewise” (John 5:19). Nor is it in glory or any rank. “For if they had known,” it says, “they would not have crucified the Lord of glory” (1 Corinthians 2:8). And it is the Father’s will, according to John, “that all should honour the Son just as they honour the Father” (John 5:23).

In what respect, then, does ‘greater’ and ‘unlike’ still hold? As has been shown, in none. And so the Apostle, checking the impious suppositions of heretics about the only-begotten Son and God, and proclaiming his identity of nature with his Father and, moreover, that he is equally without beginning, wrote, as was said above, “who, being the radiance of the glory of the Father,” and went on: “and the stamp of his hypostasis” (Hebrews 1:3).
And …

title: The Son, the Natural Image of the Father
english: … again he wrote to the Colossians and to the Hebrews: “who is the image of the invisible God” (Colossians 1:15). And in the Gospel according to John, the Son, showing that his own substance has been sealed with the Father’s stamp, said: “For on him the Father, God, has set his seal” (John 6:27).

The seal, plainly, subsists together with the archetype and bears the same impress, and in itself shows perfectly and truly the oneness of nature of the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit. For the seal, like the stamp, signifies what is like and genuine. Otherwise it would be time to say that the Father too is not ungenerated and incomparable, if he is imaged and stamped by something generated and unlike.

These divine oracles, which need no interpreter, they did not rightly understand. Twisting them, and fighting the words of God with human notions, they assert: “God is one thing and the image of God another, as a man is one thing and the image of a man another.” And in a way they liken the living and active God the Word to a motionless image. But he is the image of the Father in substance and in every respect, most exact and without beginning: not by shape and figure, like a statue moulded or carved, without breath and unable to move itself, nor by appearance and colour, like the image made by art, imitative and voiceless. For these show forth the prototype neither by nature nor indeed in all its other features.

A son of a man is indeed an image of the substance of his own father; but he may differ in age, or appearance, or disposition, or power, or rank, or in a combination of these, or in something else. But God the Word, without variation and with exactness in every respect, images the simple, uncompounded and unvaried Godhead of the Father, by nature and without beginning.

For it is not even permitted to think that he is the image of God in one respect and differs from him in another. Nor indeed can there be an image of the ‘incomparable’; nor can the true, the archetypal, the greater, the self-determining and the incomparable appear through what is unlike, or smaller, or under another’s authority; nor again can the natural form of the Creator be perceived through a creature. For no nature shows another nature in itself.

But the Father too turns out to be without hypostasis, when heretics will not grant that he has the stamp of his hypostasis. Nor does the invisible, uncompounded God, who has no figure, have an image of the imitative kind they present. And the words that follow plainly undo their views, for they run: “He did not count being equal to God a thing to be seized” (Philippians 2:6).

Moses too explains a natural image, in these words: “Adam begot Seth according to his form” (Genesis 5:3). Now Seth was of necessity not of a different substance from Adam; and yet Moses gave the name ‘form’ to this image and likeness of substance.

“But of man too,” he says, “it is written that he is ‘the image and glory of God’” (1 Corinthians 11:7). But nowhere, you people, is man or any other thing made written to be “the radiance of the glory of God and the stamp of his hypostasis” (Hebrews 1:3). It is one thing for man to be the image of God, that is, as the thing crafted is the image of its craftsman, as a stool is of the carpenter (for Solomon says: “By analogy from created things their Maker is beheld”); and it is another thing to be, in sameness of form, identity of substance and equal beginninglessness, the radiance of glory and the stamp of the hypostasis, having its own subsistence and wholly true.

For he says: “He who has seen me has seen the Father” (John 14:9). But he who has seen a man has not seen God, as one who has looked at the stool has not seen the carpenter. Indeed, it is necessary that the image of the only invisible God be alone invisible, and not man, who is visible and made after the image.

So the Son is neither like another, for it is written: “Who will be likened to the Lord among the sons of God?” (Psalm 89:6); nor unlike his own Father: “For I and the Father,” he says, “are one” (John 10:30). Those who apply to him the notion of a created image become like Nebuchadnezzar, who ordained that a manufactured, lifeless image be worshipped (Daniel 3:1-6).

God justly cast Adam out of paradise for his disobedience (Genesis 3:23-24); but the Son brought in the thief (Luke 23:43), and with him Adam and the whole common race, since he is altogether equal in Godhead, goodness and lordship to him who cast Adam out.

Where is it written that “the Father is incomparable” with his own Only-begotten, or that his Son, the Maker and Judge of all, is a “creature” in his divine nature, infinite and exalted above all things? Or at all that once “he was not”? Or where did the Father say expressly, “I created for myself a Son”? Or the Son: …

title: The Devil, Not the Son or the Spirit, Is the First Creature
english: … “I was created by the Father”? That is dreadful to hear, let alone to say, and something to flee from. Nowhere at all, then, are these things found in the divine and spiritual Scripture. On the contrary, all the sayings of the Only-begotten about his Godhead are those of one who compares himself with the Father, unites himself to him and declares himself equal in honour.

Nor has he ever been called ‘child’ or ‘little child’ or ‘offspring’ with respect to his generation above, which is infinite and which nothing whatever can describe, so that no one should imagine anything small, or anything that lends colour to their sophistical blasphemies already mentioned. He is called ‘Son’, rather, because he is perfect, because he was begotten without beginning, and because his nature does not vary from the Father’s.

All the things that some think small with respect to the Godhead, including “The Father who sent me is greater than I” (John 14:28), were uttered in the sacred books because of his loving and ineffable becoming man, which took place for our sake and on our behalf. Because of it, too, it is written that he was made lower than the angels, as the Apostle writes: “But we see Jesus, made a little lower than the angels because of the suffering of death” (Hebrews 2:9).

I think, then, and I am not altogether mistaken, that it was of the Father and himself that he spoke, showing the goodness and the oneness of substance of both: “Either make the tree good and its fruit good, or make the tree rotten and its fruit rotten; for by the fruit,” he says, “the tree is known” (Matthew 12:33).

Some, fighting against God, dare to say that the Son, and with him the Holy Spirit, is the first creature, and Macedonius says this of the Spirit alone. May the holy and consubstantial Trinity turn upon them the weight of our having to mention such mad and condemned words. For our part, we shall show from the divine Scriptures we set out that the first creature of God came to be in this way. The first creature, lifted up, was hurled down from the heavens like lightning, as he who created it well, and later justly hurled it down, beheld it in the Gospel (Luke 10:18).

And he speaks thus in Job: “But behold, a beast beside you that eats grass like oxen. Behold, its strength is in its loins, and its power on the navel of its belly. It set up its tail like a cypress, and its sinews are woven together; its ribs are bronze, and its back is cast iron. This is the beginning of the Lord’s handiwork, made to be mocked by the angels” (Job 40:15-19).

So it says that the devil is the first creature, and that he made himself a thing to be mocked by the holy angels because of the unholiness and malice of his choice. The Son, who fashioned even him, would not have been created after him; nor indeed would the Spirit of God.

On the holy Trinity: that because of the sameness of substance the same names are used alike of the hypostases, except fatherhood, sonship and the procession of the Spirit, for this is proper to each hypostasis on its own; that sometimes the Father, sometimes the Son, sometimes the Spirit is placed first; and that both the threeness and the oneness are shown in Scripture.

From all that has been said, then, it is established that their teachings are in every way foreign to the truth. For it is the work of sophistry to invent quibbles, but of wisdom to search the Scriptures with reverence and with the acceptance that befits them.

It remains necessary, then, to pass over their implausible rubbish and wrangling, and, having washed out brackish ears, as the saying goes, with the fresh, intelligible water of the Holy Spirit, to show that the Scriptures, because of the sameness of the Godhead, sometimes name one of the divine hypostases and sometimes the three, and assign the good to each of them alike. So when Moses says, “Hear, Israel: the Lord your God is one Lord” (Deuteronomy 6:4), by saying “one” he showed the one Godhead, and by “Lord”, then “God”, and again “Lord”, he signified the Trinity, from whom every good in the world and above the world has come, and will come, to mankind.

And again: “God said: Let there be a firmament; and God made the firmament; and God saw that it was good” (Genesis 1:6-8). It should be noted that he names three hypostases and calls each one God, and shows the concord and co-working of the one who spoke, the one who made and the one who praised.
And again: “God commands Moses,” it says, “saying: Speak to Aaron and to his sons: Thus you shall bless Israel …” (Numbers 6:22-23)
